scenes.narration: In some of the richest countries on Earth, the average household owes more than twice everything it earns in a year. In others, families owe barely half their income. That single number — how much a nation's households are borrowed up to the hilt — quietly decides which economies are fragile and which can weather a storm. Today we rank every major country by household debt, and reveal who's living closest to the edge.

Here's the gap that stuns people. In the most indebted countries — the Netherlands, Australia, Switzerland, Canada — households owe around two hundred percent of their yearly income, or more. In others, like much of southern and eastern Europe, it's under sixty. Same idea of a middle-class family, three times the debt load, depending on the flag.
scenes.sub: household debt as a share of income, by country

scenes.narration: So today we rank the world by household debt, break down what all that borrowing is actually for, explain why some debt builds wealth while other debt destroys it, trace how household debt quietly triggers the biggest crises in history, and show how to read your own number. Because a country's debt load, and yours, is one of the clearest predictors of financial trouble there is.

scenes.memeBottom: some debt builds wealth, some debt destroys it
scenes.narration: Because not all debt is created equal — a mortgage and a maxed-out credit card are opposites wearing the same word. Before we rank the countries, let's define what household debt really is.
First, what 'household debt' actually measures.
scenes.heading: The Debt Load

scenes.narration: Household debt is the combined debt of all people in a household, including mortgages, car loans, student loans, and credit cards. Add it up across a whole country and compare it to income, and you get a powerful gauge of financial health. The research is blunt that a sharp rise in this number has preceded many of history's worst economic crises.

And household debt is different from the government debt you usually hear about. A country can have modest national debt but households drowning in private loans — or the reverse. This is the one that lands directly on families: the mortgage payment, the car loan, the credit-card minimum. When economists want to know if ordinary people are in trouble, this is the number they watch first.

The key measure is the debt-to-income ratio — the monthly gross income that goes toward paying debts. At the household level, it tells a lender how stretched you are. At the national level, it tells you how much of a population's paycheck is already spoken for before they buy anything. The higher it climbs, the less cushion a family, or a country, has when trouble hits.

And the ratio matters more than the raw dollar amount. A family owing half a million on a mortgage but earning three hundred thousand is fine; a family owing fifty thousand on credit cards while earning forty is in crisis. The number that predicts trouble isn't how much you owe — it's how big your debt is next to what you bring in. That ratio is the whole story.

props.name: warning
props.label: small debt can be a crisis

scenes.narration: Here's the US snapshot most people never see added up. American households together owe over seventeen trillion dollars — roughly twelve trillion in mortgages, and the rest in student loans, auto loans, and credit cards. It's a debt the size of a major economy, carried on millions of ordinary kitchen tables.
scenes.sub: total US household debt — mortgages, autos, cards, loans

scenes.narration: So a high debt-to-income number isn't automatically a disaster — but it is fragility. A country where households owe two hundred percent of income can look rich and comfortable while the economy hums. But the moment interest rates rise or jobs disappear, all that debt turns from a convenience into a trap, fast. Debt is a loan against the future, and the future always eventually arrives.

Here's the leverage in one stark fact. In the most indebted countries, households owe more than two dollars for every single dollar they earn in a year. It would take them over two years of income, spending nothing on food, rent, or anything else, just to pay off what they already owe. That's how stretched the top of this ranking really is.
scenes.sub: of total income to clear the debt in top countries

scenes.narration: So let's rank the world by household debt.
scenes.heading: The Ranking

scenes.narration: One caution reading this ranking: a low number isn't automatically healthy. Some countries have little household debt simply because credit is hard to get, or because people are too poor to borrow. A thriving middle class with sensible mortgages can look more indebted than a struggling population with no access to loans at all. Context, as always, decides what the number means.

scenes.caption: household debt as a share of income, by country
scenes.narration: Here's the global leaderboard of borrowing. At the top: Switzerland, the Netherlands, Australia, and Canada, where households owe around two hundred percent of their income — often because of enormous mortgages on expensive homes. The US and UK sit lower, around a hundred. And much of southern and eastern Europe anchors the bottom, under sixty. The richest-looking countries are frequently the most leveraged.

And watch the trend, not just the level. A country whose household debt is still climbing fast is in a different place from one that's slowly paying down. Rapid, recent increases in borrowing are the real red flag economists hunt for — because it's the speed of the build-up, more than the size, that tends to precede a reckoning.

scenes.title: Household debt as % of net income
scenes.narration: Put the numbers in a row. Italy around sixty percent, Germany eighty-five, the US near a hundred, the UK a hundred and thirty, Canada one eighty-five, and the Netherlands and Australia over two hundred. The surprise for most people is that heavy household debt isn't a sign of poverty — it's often a sign of expensive housing and easy credit in wealthy nations.

And notice why the leaders are where they are. The Netherlands, Australia, Canada, and Switzerland all share expensive housing markets and easy mortgage credit. Their debt isn't reckless spending — it's the price of chasing a home in a pricey market. The ranking is, to a large degree, a map of where housing got most unaffordable, financed.

scenes.caption: what the borrowing is actually for
scenes.narration: But the raw number hides the most important thing: what the debt is for. In the heavily indebted countries, the vast majority is mortgage debt — borrowing to own a home that, hopefully, holds or grows in value. A much smaller slice is consumer debt: credit cards, car loans, and buy-now-pay-later. One of these builds a future. The other quietly dismantles it.

And the composition flips the risk entirely. A country that's heavily indebted but almost all in mortgages, on homes people actually live in, is far safer than one with lots of credit-card and consumer debt at the same total. Mortgage debt is backed by an asset and usually lower-interest. Consumer debt is backed by nothing and charges a fortune. Always ask not just how much, but what kind.

props.name: scale
props.label: ask what kind, not just how much

scenes.narration: Which brings us to the great divide: good debt versus bad.
scenes.heading: Good vs Bad Debt

scenes.narration: There's even a third category worth naming: in-between debt. A car loan buys something you genuinely need but that loses value fast. A student loan for a low-paying field is a bet that didn't pay off. Not all borrowing is cleanly good or bad — much of it depends entirely on the price you paid and the return you got. The label 'good debt' has to be earned, not assumed.

The dangerous kind is consumer debt — debt which is used to fund consumption rather than investment. It's money borrowed for things that lose value the moment you own them: restaurant meals, gadgets, vacations, financed on a card at crushing interest. This debt doesn't build anything. It just pulls your future spending into the present, and charges you brutally for the privilege.

scenes.memeTop: borrow to buy an asset that grows
scenes.memeBottom: borrow to buy stuff that's worthless by morning
scenes.narration: This is the fork that decides whether debt lifts you or sinks you. The exact same act — borrowing money — builds wealth on one path and destroys it on the other. The word 'debt' tells you nothing. What you bought with it tells you everything.

Contrast that with a mortgage or a student loan for a high-paying field. That's borrowing to acquire an asset — a home, or earning power — that can grow and pay you back over time. The debt is large, but it's working for you. The country that owes two hundred percent in mortgages is in a very different position from one drowning in credit-card balances, even at the same total.

scenes.memeTop: minimum payments on five maxed-out cards
scenes.narration: For households deep in high-interest consumer debt, this is the quiet treadmill: paying every month, watching the balance barely move, as interest eats most of each payment. It isn't a spending problem you can shrug off — it's a trap engineered to keep you paying forever. Recognizing it is the first step off the treadmill.
And here's why this ranking really matters: crises.
scenes.heading: The Debt Bomb

scenes.narration: And debt crises have a terrifying feature: they're contagious. When overindebted households stop paying, banks take losses, so they lend less, so businesses cut jobs, so more households can't pay. One group's debt problem becomes everyone's economic problem. That chain reaction is why a number on a spreadsheet about private borrowing can end up on the front page as a global recession.

At its core, debt is an obligation that requires you to pay money borrowed or otherwise withheld from another party. That obligation doesn't care about your circumstances. When a whole nation's households are maxed out and a shock hits — a rate hike, a recession, a housing dip — millions can't pay at once. That synchronized failure is exactly how household debt turns into a national catastrophe.

And the cruelest feature of debt is that it's rigid while life is not. Your income can fall, your hours can get cut, a recession can hit — but the loan payment stays exactly the same. That rigidity is why debt amplifies every downturn. In good times it's invisible; in bad times, it's the thing that turns a rough patch into a catastrophe.

scenes.caption: debt climbs, then the crash
scenes.narration: This is the pattern behind two thousand eight and nearly every crisis like it. Household debt climbs for years as credit gets easy and home prices soar. Everyone feels wealthy. Then rates rise or prices wobble, the borrowing can't be sustained, and the whole thing snaps. The higher a country let household debt climb, the harder and faster that snap tends to be.

Say the 2008 lesson plainly. US household debt climbed to record highs on easy mortgages in the mid-two-thousands — then home prices fell, millions couldn't pay, and the synchronized collapse nearly took down the entire global financial system. It wasn't government debt that lit the fuse. It was households, borrowed to the limit, all breaking at once.
scenes.sub: household debt, not government debt, lit the fuse

scenes.narration: The painful cure is deleveraging — the reduction of the leverage ratio, as households scramble to pay down debt all at once. But when everyone stops spending to pay off loans simultaneously, the economy seizes up. It's a brutal, years-long hangover. The highly indebted countries aren't necessarily doomed — but they're the ones with the least room to maneuver when the music stops.

And rising interest rates are the modern trigger to watch. Much of that two-hundred-percent debt sits on variable-rate or soon-to-reset mortgages. When central banks hike rates, those payments jump, sometimes by hundreds a month, with no warning. Highly indebted countries like Canada and Australia are especially exposed — their households feel every rate rise almost immediately.
So how do you read your own number — and stay safe?
scenes.heading: What To Do

scenes.narration: And if you're carrying bad debt, use the two proven ways out. The avalanche method kills your highest-interest debt first, saving the most money. The snowball method clears your smallest balance first, for a motivating quick win. Pick whichever you'll actually stick with — the best debt-payoff plan is simply the one you don't abandon halfway through.

Start by calculating your own debt-to-income ratio: your monthly debt payments divided by your monthly income. Under about thirty-six percent is healthy; past forty-three, lenders get nervous and so should you. That one number tells you, honestly, how much of your life is already pledged to the past. Everyone should know it, and almost nobody does.

And build the one thing debt steals: a buffer. Debt is dangerous mainly because it leaves no room for shocks. An emergency fund, even a small one, is what lets you keep paying through a job loss or a surprise bill without spiraling into more borrowing. The indebted who survive crises are almost always the ones who kept a little cash between themselves and the edge.

Then sort your debt. Attack the bad debt — credit cards and high-interest consumer loans — with everything you've got, because that's the debt actively making you poorer. Be comfortable with sensible good debt, like an affordable mortgage, that's buying a real asset. The goal was never zero debt. It's owning more than you owe, with the right kind of debt in between.

And borrow for your future self, not against them. Before taking on any new debt, ask one question: will this still be paying me back long after the payments end? A home, an education that raises your income, a tool that earns — yes. A nicer car, a vacation, a gadget on a card — no. That single question quietly sorts the debt that builds lives from the debt that wrecks them.

props.name: chartup
props.label: will it still pay you back?

scenes.narration: Because here's the real lesson. A country, or a person, drowning in debt can look identical to a wealthy one right up until the moment the bill comes due. Debt borrows prosperity from tomorrow to spend today — and the ranking we just saw is really a map of who will struggle most when tomorrow arrives. Watch the debt, not just the lifestyle. It tells you who's actually rich, and who only looks it.

And zoom out on the quiet trade every borrower makes. Debt is simply time travel for money: it moves future earnings into the present. Used to buy an asset that outgrows the interest, that time travel makes you richer. Used to buy things that vanish, it makes your future self poorer to please your present self. The whole game is making sure the trade is worth it.

props.name: chartup
props.label: worth it if the asset outgrows it
